name: Himeji Castle
info: Himeji Castle is a hilltop castle complex of 83 structures in Himeji, Hyōgo Prefecture, Japan, first fortified in 1333 and rebuilt on its present scale by Ikeda Terumasa between 1601 and 1609.

facts.made: Fortified by Akamatsu Norimura in 1333, remodelled by the Kuroda clan and by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, rebuilt by Ikeda Terumasa from 1601 to 1609 and extended by Honda Tadamasa from 1617 to 1618
facts.form: A hirayama (flat hilltop) castle of stone and wood with white plaster walls: a main keep 46.4 metres high with three smaller keeps, 83 buildings, three moats and a spiral approach, on a complex of 233 hectares
facts.where: On the hill called Himeyama, 45.6 metres above sea level, in the centre of Himeji, Hyōgo Prefecture, Japan
facts.known: the white plaster exterior that gave it the names Hakuro-jō and Shirasagi-jō; the maze of paths to the keep; roughly 1,000 loopholes; five National Treasures; survival of the 1945 bombing and the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake; registration as a World Heritage Site in 1993

t: The hill was first fortified in 1333, and the castle seen today was largely built by Ikeda Terumasa between 1601 and 1609, a work believed to have taken 2.5 million man-days of labour.
Its gates, baileys and walls were laid out so that an approaching force would travel in a spiral, but the castle was never attacked in this manner and the system remains untested.

It was spared demolition in the Meiji Period, survived the bombing of Himeji in 1945 and the Great Hanshin earthquake of 1995, and was registered in 1993 as one of the first World Heritage Sites in Japan.
dyk: The straight distance from the Hishi Gate to the main keep is only 130 metres, but the path between them is 325 metres long.
ev: Akamatsu Norimura fortified Himeyama hill during the Genkō War
His son Sadanori demolished the fort and built Himeyama Castle in its place
Toyotomi Hideyoshi expanded the castle and built a three-storey keep
Ikeda Terumasa began to rebuild the castle completely, work that lasted until 1609
Honda Tadamasa inherited the castle and added several buildings, including the Dressing Tower for Princess Sen
The castle was abandoned and the whole complex was slated for demolition, but Nakamura Shigeto spared it
Himeji was heavily bombed, and the castle survived intact
The castle was registered as one of the first World Heritage Sites in Japan

sections.origins:
Himeyama hill, the site of present-day Himeji Castle, was first fortified in 1333 by Akamatsu Norimura, the shugo of Harima Province, during the Genkō War. In 1346 his son Sadanori demolished this fort and built Himeyama Castle in its place. In 1545 the Kuroda clan was stationed here by order of the Kodera clan, and the feudal ruler Kuroda Shigetaka remodelled the castle into Himeji Castle, completing the work in 1561.

In 1580 Kuroda Yoshitaka presented the castle to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who in 1581 expanded it significantly and built a three-storey keep with an area of about 55 square metres. After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu granted the castle to his son-in-law Ikeda Terumasa as a reward for his help in the battle. The complex stands on a hill called Himeyama in the centre of Himeji, and its style is hirayama, a flat hilltop castle. Matsuyama Castle (Iyo) and Tsuyama Castle were built at the same time and share many of its architectural features.
sections.content:
The castle complex is a network of 83 buildings, among them storehouses, gates, corridors and turrets (yagura). The main keep (daitenshu) at its centre is 46.4 metres high and stands 92 metres above sea level; with three smaller subsidiary keeps it forms a cluster of towers. From outside the keep appears to have five floors, because the second and third floors from the top look like a single one, but it has six floors and a basement. As in almost all Japanese castles from the Azuchi-Momoyama period onward, the keep was used as a storehouse in peacetime and as a fortified tower in war, while the daimyo's offices and residences stood in single-storey buildings nearby.

The first floor measures 554 square metres and is often called the thousand-mat room because it holds over 330 tatami mats. Its walls carry weapon racks for matchlocks and spears, and at one point the castle held as many as 280 guns and 90 spears. The third and fourth floors have stone-throwing platforms at the north and south windows and small enclosed rooms called warrior hiding places, where defenders could wait and kill attackers by surprise as they entered the keep. The principal materials are stone and wood, and feudal family crests (kamon) set throughout the buildings mark the lords who lived there.
sections.making:
Ikeda Terumasa demolished the three-storey keep that Hideyoshi had built in 1581 and rebuilt and expanded the castle from 1601 to 1609. He added three moats and made it the complex seen today. The labour involved in the expansion is believed to have totalled 2.5 million man-days. Ikeda died in 1613 and passed the castle to his son, who died three years later. In 1617 Honda Tadamasa and his family inherited it, and Honda added several buildings, including a special tower for his daughter-in-law, Princess Sen, called the keshō yagura (Dressing Tower).

The main keep has two pillars, one in the east and one in the west. The east pillar, with a base diameter of 97 centimetres, was originally a single fir tree but has since been mostly replaced. The west pillar is of Japanese cypress. In the Shōwa Restoration of 1956 to 1964 a cypress 26.4 metres long was brought down from the Kiso Mountains to replace the old west pillar; the tree broke in the process, so another was brought down from Mount Kasagata and the two were joined on the third floor. The legend of the master carpenter Sakurai Genbei says that he judged the keep to lean a little to the southeast and, distraught, jumped to his death from its top with a chisel in his mouth.
sections.reception:
The castle is known as Hakuro-jō or Shirasagi-jō, the White Egret Castle or White Heron Castle, for its white exterior and its supposed resemblance to a bird taking flight. It is the largest castle in Japan and is considered, with Matsumoto Castle and Kumamoto Castle, one of the country's three premier castles. It is regarded as the finest surviving example of prototypical Japanese castle architecture. Its defences were designed to let defenders fire from the keep on intruders during a long approach, but the castle was never attacked in this manner, so the system remains untested.

Local legends are attached to the castle. Banshū Sarayashiki, a variant of the ghost story Banchō Sarayashiki set in Edo, is set at Himeji, where an alleged Okiku's Well remains; the claim that the castle is the true location of the whole legend is disputed. In the tale Okiku was falsely accused of losing valuable dishes and was killed and thrown into the well, and her ghost counts the dishes at night. The yōkai Osakabehime is said to live in the keep and to avoid humans. According to the legend of the Old Widow's Stone, an old woman gave Hideyoshi her millstone when he ran short of stones, and others followed her example.
sections.survival:
In the Meiji Period many Japanese castles were destroyed. Himeji Castle was abandoned in 1871, and some of its corridors and gates were destroyed to make room for army barracks. The whole complex was slated for demolition by government policy but was spared through the efforts of an army colonel, Nakamura Shigeto, who is honoured by a stone monument inside the Hishi Gate. When the han system was abolished in 1871 the castle was designated for military use in 1872, and by 1874 it briefly served as headquarters of the 10th Infantry Regiment. Efforts to preserve it began in 1877, but government funding for a comprehensive restoration came only in 1910.

Himeji was heavily bombed in 1945, and although most of the surrounding area was burned to the ground, the castle survived intact. One firebomb fell on the top floor and failed to explode. Substantial repair work began in 1956, with 250,000 man-days of labour and a cost of 550 million yen. In January 1995 the Great Hanshin earthquake substantially damaged the city, but the castle survived virtually undamaged, and even the bottle of sake on the altar of the top floor stayed in place. A further restoration began in April 2010 and ended with the reopening on 27 March 2015; it removed decades of dirt and grime and restored the formerly grey roof to its white colour.
sections.legacy:
Himeji Castle was registered on 11 December 1993 as one of the first World Heritage Sites in Japan. Five of its structures are National Treasures: the main keep, the northwest, west and east small keeps, and the I, Ro, Ha and Ni corridors with the kitchen. The area within the middle moat is a Special Historic Site. Of the 83 buildings, 74 are designated Important Cultural Assets: 11 corridors, 16 turrets, 15 gates and 32 earthen walls. Matsumoto, Inuyama, Matsue and Hikone castles are also National Treasures, and Himeji's sister castles are the Château de Chantilly in France and Conwy Castle in Wales.

Beside the castle lies Kōko-en, a Japanese garden created in 1992 to commemorate the hundredth anniversary of Himeji city. The complex has a circumference of 4,200 metres, and parts of the central moat and all of the inner moats survive, along with 21 of its original 84 gates and 13 of its 33 wells.

summary: Himeji Castle in Hyōgo Prefecture was first fortified in 1333 and rebuilt on its present scale by Ikeda Terumasa from 1601 to 1609. It escaped demolition in the Meiji Period, the bombing of 1945 and the 1995 earthquake, and was registered as a World Heritage Site in 1993.
references: Oleg and Ran Zwigenberg Benesch, Japan's Castles: Citadels of Modernity in War and Peace (Cambridge University Press, 2019)
William De Lange, An Encyclopedia of Japanese Castles (Toyo Press, 2021)
Morton S. Schmorleitz, Castles in Japan (Charles E. Tuttle Co., 1974)
notes: The article gives the building history in layers (1333 fort, 1346 Himeyama Castle, 1561 Himeji Castle, 1581, 1601-1609); start 1333 is the first fortification, with the present complex dating from 1601-1609.
The article says 'For almost 700 years' the castle has remained intact; not used.
Left out: visitor numbers, the Lego model, video games, the Visitor statistics section (tourism/'as of' material).
The Meiji paragraph of the article dates abandonment to 1871 and military designation to 1872; both used.
Lore (Okiku, Osakabehime, Ubagaishi, Sakurai Genbei) is given as legend, as the article gives it.
The 'Shōwa Restoration' is given in the article as 1956-1964; the 1956 start also appears in the 1945 paragraph.
